opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I think about it a lot. Right now, agents.md is basically a way for you to give the agent the context it can't easily figure out on its own: how you run tests, the conventions your team cares about, which parts of the codebase are fragile, that kind of thing. It's a very simple mechanism. It's just a file in your repo, and that simplicity is a big part of why it works. It's versioned with your code, everyone on the team can see it and edit it, and it's portable across tools.

As agents get better memory, I think some of what people put in agents.md today will become unnecessary. If the agent has worked in your codebase a hundred times, it should just know that you use a particular test runner, or that you always want a certain lint step before committing. You shouldn't have to write that down. The agent should learn it the way a new teammate does after their first few weeks.

But I don't think it goes away. I think its role shifts. There's a difference between what an agent picks up implicitly and what a team wants to state explicitly. Memory is great for learned preferences and accumulated context, but it can be opaque. You don't always know what the model has remembered or why it's behaving a certain way. agents.md is the opposite. It's explicit, reviewable, and shared. So I see it becoming more like the place for intent and policy: "This is how we want things done here," the non-negotiables, the architectural decisions, the things you want to be true no matter which agent or which person is working on the code.

There's also an interesting loop that could emerge, where the agent notices patterns in how you work and proposes updates to agents.md: "I've seen you correct me on this three times. Should I write it down?" Then the human stays in control of what becomes codified, while the agent does the tedious work of keeping it up to date.

So the short version: memory handles more of the implicit stuff, and agents.md becomes more focused, more about shared, explicit agreements between the team and the agents working alongside them.

r001.rationale: The response says agents.md supplies context the agent cannot easily figure out on its own, such as test commands and team conventions.

r002.rationale: It connects agents.md’s current role to what agents do not yet know, then says better memory would make some of that written guidance unnecessary.

r003.rationale: The response describes agents remembering recurring codebase practices, but does not identify reusing previously solved problems across repeated runs as a memory research goal.

r004.rationale: The response mentions accumulated codebase context, but does not identify reusing understanding gained through codebase exploration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about a lot. I'd say agents.md today is doing two jobs at once, and better memory is going to pull those two jobs apart.

The first job is onboarding. When you drop an agent into a repo cold, it doesn't know your build commands, it doesn't know that you run tests with a particular flag, it doesn't know that one directory is legacy and shouldn't be touched. Agents.md is where a human writes that down, the same way you'd write a README for a new teammate. The second job is correction. The agent did something you didn't like, so you add a line saying "don't do that," and over time the file accumulates these little scars from past mistakes.

As agents get real memory, that second job mostly goes away from the file. If the agent remembers that last week you told it to stop reformatting the whole file when it touches one function, you shouldn't have to write that down. It should just learn it, and ideally learn it per person, because what I want and what my colleague wants are often different, and a single shared file flattens that.

But I don't think the first job goes away, and I actually think it becomes more important. Memory is private and accumulated. Agents.md is shared and intentional. It's the thing the team agrees on, it's version controlled, it goes through code review, you can diff it. When a new engineer joins, or when you switch to a different agent, or when a model gets upgraded and its priors shift a bit, that file is the stable ground truth. Memory is what the agent picked up along the way. Agents.md is what the team decided.

So the way I'd put it is that the file gets shorter and more deliberate. Less "here are forty things I noticed you doing wrong," more "here is how this project works and what we care about." And then there's an interesting layer in between, where the agent can propose edits to agents.md based on what it's learned. It notices that three different people have corrected it the same way, and it says, hey, this looks like a team convention, should we write it down? That's the loop I'm most excited about, memory feeding back into the shared, explicit contract rather than replacing it.

The one thing I'd caution against is letting memory become a place where important context hides. If the agent only works well because of a long private history of corrections, that's fragile. The stuff that matters should surface somewhere people can see it and argue about it. Agents.md is a pretty good place for that to live.

r001.rationale: It says agents.md onboards an agent dropped into a repo by supplying build commands, test flags, and other context the agent otherwise lacks.

r002.rationale: It links agents.md’s current role to agents lacking context when they start cold, then explains how better memory could take over the correction role.

r003.rationale: It discusses remembering past corrections, but does not identify reusing previously solved problems across repeated runs as a memory research goal.

r004.rationale: It does not describe memory reusing understanding gained through codebase exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think agents.md will become less of a place where you have to explain everything upfront, and more of a place where you express intent: how you want the agent to work, what matters for this project, what constraints it should respect.

As memory improves, the agent should be able to pick up recurring preferences and retain lessons from previous work, so you don’t have to keep repeating yourself. But there’s still value in an explicit file that you can read, edit, and share with your team. You want to distinguish between something the agent inferred from an interaction and something you deliberately established as a project rule.

So I see them as complementary. Memory helps the agent adapt over time; agents.md gives you a clear way to steer that adaptation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents.md is an early way of giving an agent persistent context: here’s how this repository works, here are the conventions, here’s how you run the tests. As memory improves, the agent should be able to learn more of that through working with you, so you don’t have to write everything down or repeat the same correction every session.

But I don’t think that makes agents.md disappear. There’s a useful distinction between what the agent has learned and what you explicitly want it to follow. A file gives the team something shared, visible, and version controlled. My expectation is that memory will make those files less exhaustive, while they remain a place to express deliberate instructions. The important part is making it easy to understand and correct what the agent remembers.

r001.rationale: It says agents.md supplies repository structure, conventions, and test instructions, giving the agent context it would otherwise need to acquire.

r002.rationale: It presents agents.md as an early source of persistent context and contrasts that role with agents’ improving memory.

r003.rationale: It mentions avoiding repeated corrections across sessions, but does not identify reusing previously solved problems as a memory research goal.

r004.rationale: It describes learning through working with the user, but does not identify reusing understanding gained through codebase exploration as a memory research goal.
